subject: english-literature
title: Bhabha, Achebe and Hybridity
welcome_lead: From Bhabha's third space to Achebe's polemic — survey post-colonial concepts of mixture, mimicry and writing back.
meta_desc: Bhabha's hybridity, mimicry and Achebe on Conrad at A-Level English Literature.
final_note: You have toured post-colonial concepts of hybridity, mimicry and the counter-discursive — empire answered back.

concepts.def: Homi Bhabha (The Location of Culture, 1994) — the productive in-between of colonial cultures.
Bhabha — the colonised's partial imitation of the coloniser, producing 'almost the same but not quite'.
Bhabha's term for the in-between zone where identities are negotiated and remade.
Chinua Achebe's 1975 lecture branded Heart of Darkness racist, reframing canonical reception.
Post-colonial novelists rewrite canonical texts (Rhys's Wide Sargasso Sea reworks Jane Eyre).
Texts that contest the assumptions of dominant discourse — Achebe's Things Fall Apart against colonial fictions of Africa.

walkthroughs.h2: Almost the Same but Not Quite
walkthroughs.body_html: Bhabha argues colonial authority demands the colonised resemble the coloniser but not exactly. Mimicry preserves and destabilises that authority at once.

Achebe's 1975 lecture 'An Image of Africa' argued Heart of Darkness depended on dehumanising African presence.

The lecture reframed Conrad's reception and helped institutionalise post-colonial criticism.
Jean Rhys's Wide Sargasso Sea (1966) gives Bertha Mason from Jane Eyre a Caribbean voice and prehistory — writing back at its most architectural.
